title: The PR: evidence, judge, Byte and the ready gate

story: RH-1234's work is done. The self-review receipt says found 6, fixed 5, left 1: the new card still flashes for one render while the table is loading, and that question is waiting for you, the requester, in Slack. Now Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent, writes the pull request description, and it writes like a proud author: "A workgroup with no projects now sees a No projects yet card. Handles the loading state too, so the card never flashes. Tested at 760 and 1440 pixels wide."

Dana, a teammate, reads it at four in the afternoon, between two meetings. The words sound careful, so she reads the diff quickly and approves. Two of those sentences are false. The flash is exactly the item that was left open, and every video was recorded at 1440 pixels; nobody looked at 760. Nova did not lie on purpose. After an hour of work, a model describes the change the way it hoped the change would be.
hook.question: How do we make every sentence in an agent's PR description something a reviewer can trust?

read.h: Facts from files, words from the model
p: The run already knows the truth about RH-1234. It is in the evidence pack, which is everything the run collected as proof: the before run (the new tests failing on the unchanged code) and the after run, a short video for each check that a person can see on screen, the table of checks Nova ran and skipped, the self-review receipt, and a link to the trace, the record of every step and model call. The pack lives in the .nova folder on the branch and in the runs bucket, the S3 bucket where each run keeps its files. So the question is not where the facts are. The question is who copies them into the description. If the model writes the whole body, every fact passes through its memory of a long session, and that memory is hopeful, as the story showed.

That is why the body is split by who may write which part. render(), a plain function in the harness (our program in the VM that runs Nova's session), copies every fact straight from the pack: one row for each QA check, showing its result and a link to its proof, the before and after runs, the checks Nova chose not to run with a reason for each, the risk from the approved plan, the receipt, and the last line, Requested-by: @sean, which the independent-approval check reads so that it can refuse an approval from the person who asked. The model writes only three short pieces of prose: what changes, why, and where to look first. A "pass" in the table can never be a hopeful guess, because the model never types it.

code.file: harness/src/pr-body.mjs (shortened, the same shape as the lab)

notes.text: The facts. The harness wrote these files during the run, from test reports, the QA agent's results and the receipt.
The model's part: three short pieces of prose and nothing else.
The result comes from the QA results file. A check that never ran says "not run", never pass.
The skipped checks, each with its reason. "- None." when nothing was skipped, so a heading is never left empty.
Written from the run's requester and the people file, never by the model. A missing or wrong line would break the approval rule.

deeper.h: Go deeper: the same headings on every PR
p: The headings come from one shared PR template for the whole team, the pr-story template: What changes, Why, How it was checked, What was not checked and why, Risk and rollback, Where to look first, then a folded details block and the references. Because every PR has the same headings, a reviewer from the backend guild who opens a frontend PR knows where the proof is without reading everything. "What was not checked, and why" is the most honest heading of all: it is where Nova says that it looked at 1440 and not at 760, and why that was its choice.

Proof is linked, never pasted. GitHub has no API for attaching files to a pull request, so each video or screenshot is a link to the runs bucket through a small viewer that asks you to log in; the bucket itself is never public. Pictures appear only where the QA plan asked for them: a video of 30 seconds or less for a flow, screenshots at 760 and 1440 for layout, plain text for API and command-line output. They show seed data only, the fake data that test copies of the product are filled with, and never pictures of code or logs. The Jira ticket gets a short comment in the same voice: the status, the PR link and what was found.

Some rules about the body have nothing to do with meaning, so a script checks them, the way the plan schema checked its own rules in the lesson on plans. Every heading is there and in order. The part above the fold, which means everything a reviewer sees before the folded details block, stays under about 300 words. Every check marked pass has a link to proof. No long log is pasted into the body. The last line is Requested-by: and a login. A rule that a script can check should never cost a model call, and it should never depend on a model being in a good mood.

Look at what this leaves out. In the lab, the shape check passes on RH-1234's body while the first paragraph still says "Tested at 760 and 1440 pixels wide". A script can see that the sentence exists. It cannot see that the sentence is false, because the truth is spread over three places: the claim in the prose, the list of skipped checks, and the proof links, which all end in -1440. Comparing a claim with the evidence is reading, and reading needs a judge.

read.h: A judge that reads like the other team
p: The PR judge is a separate model session that reads the description the way a reviewer from another team would: someone who did not write the change and does not know the area. It reads the description first, as on GitHub, and then checks every claim, which here means any sentence that says something is true about the change. For each one it asks three questions. Is it in the diff? ("Handles the loading state" means a loading state must be there.) Is there proof? (A check marked pass needs a test run, a video or a transcript in the pack.) Would I understand it without opening the Jira ticket?

What the judge gets decides what it can catch. It gets the description, the diff and the evidence pack, and never Nova's transcript, because a reader who knows what Nova meant is kind to unclear words. Its tools are Read, Grep and Glob, without Bash, because a command such as git diff --output= can write files, so the harness writes the diff to a file before the judge starts. Its answer is structured output, the JSON-that-must-match-a-schema you know from the lesson on judges: ready or not, and a list of items, each with the sentence, the problem and a suggested rewrite. Its prompt also says that a clear, true description with nothing to flag is a good result, because a reader told to find problems always finds some.

Every proof link ends in -1440 and the skipped list names 760, so there is no proof for 760.

deeper.h: Go deeper: the verdict schema, the second round and calibration
p: The verdict's shape is a zod schema converted to JSON Schema with target "draft-7", because the SDK validates with draft-07 and refuses the newer draft that zod writes by default. The problem field is one of five fixed words: unclear, not_in_diff, no_proof, missing (a heading or a needed fact is absent) and too_long.

Nova rewrites the sentences the judge flagged and the judge reads the new description again, in a fresh session. If the same item comes back a second time, it does not get a third round: it stays in the PR as a note for the reviewer, because two rounds of disagreement mean a person should read that sentence closely. Before the judge is trusted, it runs on 10 past pull requests that people wrote and 10 Nova drafts with false claims planted in them. It must catch the planted claims without flagging most of the human PRs, because a judge that complains about every description teaches everyone to ignore it.

Only a description that the judge accepts is published, and even then nobody hears about it yet. Through the broker, the service that holds our GitHub credentials, Nova opens PR #2512 as a draft, with the title [FE] RH-1234: Empty projects table shows a No projects yet card. Byte, our review agent, reviews drafts that Nova opens, as you saw in the lesson on Byte, and posts only new important findings. For each one, Nova either fixes it and replies "Fixed in" and the commit, or replies with its reason for disagreeing, because Byte can be wrong too. Byte's findings get the same fingerprints as the self-review's, short hashes that recognise the same finding at a new line, so a finding that comes back after a fix goes to you, the requester, in Slack instead of going round again. Each push runs CI again by itself; Nova never re-runs or starts a CI workflow.

Then the ready gate, the last check before Nova marks a PR ready (you met it in the lesson on agent PRs), reads the facts: the required checks, every QA result, both judges, and the findings that are still open. One case needs care. If main itself fails the same check, no change on this branch can make it green, so Nova links main's failing run in the PR as proof and flags it for a person instead of looping. When everything is clean, Nova marks the PR ready, the frontend reviewers are asked for a review, you get one Slack message, and the ticket is assigned back to you. The reviewer now opens a PR whose every sentence was checked against the evidence, and whose last line names the one person who may not approve it.

lab.title: A PR body that cannot overclaim
lab.goal: Render RH-1234's PR body from an evidence pack so every fact comes from a file, check its shape with a script, and see which false sentences only a judge can catch.

guess.q: Nova's prose says "Tested at 760 and 1440 pixels wide", but every video in the evidence pack was recorded at 1440. The body has every heading, a proof link on every pass and a Requested-by line. Will a script that checks the body's shape catch the false sentence?

options.text: Yes, because the shape check reads every line of the body.
options.why: It reads every line, but only for form: headings, word count, links, the last line. Whether a sentence is true is not a question of form.

options.text: No, because the sentence is well formed; only a reader that compares it with the evidence sees that it is false.
options.why: The truth is spread over the claim, the skipped list and the proof links. Comparing them is reading, which is the PR judge's job.

options.text: No, because the sentence is in the folded details block, which the script skips.
options.why: The sentence is in What changes, at the very top. The script would see it; it just cannot judge it.

lab.build: Add the missing section to render.mjs, right after the line with the before and after links: a "### What was not checked, and why" heading, then one line per entry in ev.checks.skipped written as "name: why", using the lines() helper so an empty list prints "- None.". Run node render.mjs > pr.md && node shape.mjs pr.md until it prints the shape is right, then run the grep again: a third line appears, the skipped check at 760. Finally, act as the judge: rewrite what_changes in story.json so that every sentence is true for this evidence, render again, and check the shape once more.

lab.fix: Last week someone decided render() was "too much code" and asked the model to write the whole body in one go. The result is handwritten.md. Run node shape.mjs handwritten.md and read the four problems. For each one, name the line of render.mjs that makes that mistake impossible. Then find the two sentences in handwritten.md that only a judge would flag, "Everything is fully tested and all edge cases are handled" and "RH-1234 asked for it.", and write the PR judge's item for each: the sentence, the problem word (no_proof or unclear), and a true rewrite.
explain: Why does code, and not the model, write the checks table and the Requested-by line?
The shape check passes, but the description is still false. What does the PR judge compare that the script cannot?
Why does the judge read the description, the diff and the evidence pack, but never Nova's transcript?
lab.done: pr.md passes the shape check, its prose says only what the evidence supports, and you can say which mistakes code prevents and which only the judge can see.

check.q: Why does render() copy the checks table from the evidence pack instead of letting the model write it?

options.text: Models cannot write Markdown tables reliably
options.why: They write tables well. The problem is the content of the table, not its format.

options.text: A result copied from the run's own files cannot drift from what really happened, while a result the model types passes through its hopeful memory
options.why: The model never types pass or fail. If a check failed or never ran, the table says so, whatever the prose hopes.
The length is about the same. What changes is who is allowed to state a fact.

check.q: The shape check passes on RH-1234's body, but What changes still says "Tested at 760 and 1440 pixels wide" and every video is at 1440. Who catches it before a reviewer reads it?

options.text: The ready gate, because it reads the QA results
options.why: The gate reads results, and all three checks really passed. It never reads the prose, so a false sentence about widths goes straight past it.

options.text: The shape check, once you add a rule for the word 760
options.why: A rule for one word catches one sentence. The next description will overclaim in other words; comparing claims with evidence needs a reader.

options.text: The PR judge, which checks each claim against the diff and the evidence and flags it as no_proof
options.why: The judge sees the claim, the skipped list and the proof links together, and asks for a rewrite before the PR leaves draft.

check.q: A teammate suggests giving the PR judge Nova's transcript "so it understands what Nova meant". What do you answer?

options.text: No: the judge must read only what a reviewer will read, plus the diff and the proof, or it becomes kind to unclear and false sentences
options.why: The reviewer will not have the transcript. A judge that knows the intent fills gaps that a real reader cannot.

options.text: Yes, because more context always gives a better verdict
options.why: For a judge, context is not neutral. Nova's reasoning is exactly what the judge must not be persuaded by.

options.text: Yes, but only the last hour of it, to keep the prompt small
options.why: Size is not the problem. Any part of the reasoning makes the judge read what Nova meant instead of what Nova wrote.

p: The body is rendered by harness/src/pr-body.ts from .nova/plan.json, checks.json, qa_results.json, receipt.json and the trace link (G4-20). It uses the pr-story headings, which replace fcp's four-section .github/pull_request_template.md instead of adding a second template, and it keeps ### References with the Jira link, so fcp's add-jira-links.yml finds it and leaves the body alone. The Requested-by login comes from config/people.yaml. How the viewer for proof links is served is still to decide with DevOps.

The PR judge is harness/prompts/pr-judge.md, run as its own query() on Sonnet 5.5 at medium with a zod verdict schema converted with { target: "draft-7" } (G4-21). Nova opens the draft through the broker from the run's branch, nova/RH-1234 (the ticket uses a nova/RH-1234-<slug> branch, which the broker would refuse, so it must change), and requests the byte team; a person changes fcp's byte-review.yml with Nave so Byte sees Nova's drafts (G4-26). The ready gate, orchestrator/src/activities/ready-gate.ts, reads gh pr checks --required through the broker; it must leave the independent-approval check out by name, because that check cannot pass before a person approves a draft that nobody is asked to review (G4-27).

tickets.why: The evidence pack and render(): facts from files, prose from the model, the pr-story headings and the Requested-by line.
The PR judge: its prompt, its inputs, its verdict schema, the second round and its calibration.
The draft PR, Byte's review and the fix-or-answer loop with fingerprints.
The ready gate and the single round of pings when the PR is clean.

words.plain: Everything a run collected as proof: before and after runs, videos, the checks table, the receipt and the trace link.
A sentence in the description that says something is true about the change.
The top of the PR body that a reviewer sees before the folded details; kept under about 300 words.
The shared PR headings, the same on every PR, so any reviewer knows where the proof is.
A separate session that checks each claim in the description against the diff and the evidence.

review.q: From memory: which parts of the PR body does code write, and which three does the model write?
review.a: Code writes the checks table with results and proof links, the before and after links, what was not checked and why, the risk, the receipt, the cost and time, the references and the Requested-by line. The model writes what changes, why, and where to look first.

review.q: Name three rules about the body that a script checks, and one kind of mistake only the judge can see.
review.a: All headings in order, under about 300 words above the fold, a proof link on every pass, no pasted logs, Requested-by as the last line. Only the judge sees a well-formed sentence that the diff or the evidence does not support.

review.q: The judge flags the same sentence in two rounds in a row. What happens, and why not a third round?
review.a: The item stays in the PR as a note for the reviewer. Two rounds of disagreement mean a person should read that sentence closely; more rounds would only repeat the argument.

remember: Let code copy every fact from the evidence pack, let the model write only the story, and let a judge that never saw the transcript check each claim before anyone is pinged.
